newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain to protest China plans for Hong Kong laws.
newsitem.headline: Britain to protest China plans for Hong Kong laws.

text.p: Britain is preparing to protest against China's plans to water down laws guaranteeing civil liberties in Hong Kong after Beijing takes over the British colony in July, Governor Chris Patten said on Tuesday.
The proposals to amend or repeal a list of 25 laws and ordinances has prompted a storm of protest in the territory and stoked fears that China may seek to snuff out further freedoms.
Pro-democracy groups described China's proposals as a blow to democracy and human rights that would dent international confidence in post-1997 Hong Kong.

"We are discussing with London the diplomatic steps that we will now take, that will include of course raising our very deep concerns through the Joint Liaison Group machinery, but we will be going further than that," Patten told reporters.
Chinese and British diplomats appointed to the Joint Liaison Group (JLG) meet regularly to thrash out transitional issues.

Fears that China might embark down this particular track have been lurking since Beijing exploded in fury over democratic reforms spearheaded by Patten, who arrived in 1992 to lead Hong Kong through the changeover.
Sino-British relations nosedived and Chinese suspicion deepened about virtually every change put in place by the British in the twilight of colonial rule.
China has already chosen a provisional legislature to replace the elected body returned in 1995 under the auspices of the Patten reforms.

On Sunday, a legal panel of the China-appointed Preparatory Committee responsible for transforming the British colony into a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China drew up a list of laws and regulations it wants to reverse or amend.

At the top of the list were Patten's electoral reforms that broadened democracy and human rights legislation passed during Patten's stewardship to bring Hong Kong in line with the U.N. Convenant on Civil and Political Rights.

The Chinese-language Sing Tao Daily slammed the proposals, which it said would cause panic. The Apple Daily deplored the move "as a major political step backward which cleared the way for dictatorship".
China argues that some clauses in the human rights ordinances conflict with the Basic Law, the post-1997 constitution for Hong Kong promulgated by Beijing in 1990.
Chinese delegate to the JLG, Chen Zuo'er, praised the proposals for "putting history back on the right track".
Pro-Beijing politician Selina Chow said she saw no conflict between the existing laws and the Basic Law, but most members of the Provisional Legislature defended the proposals.

"I don't think the allegations that by changing these laws, the state of human rights in Hong Kong after the handover will be much worse than now or before is well founded," said pro-Beijing politician Tsang Yok-shing.

The Provisional Legislature holds its first formal session on Saturday just over the border from Hong Kong in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. It is expected to begin work on repealing and redrafting the 25 laws and articles.

Hong Kong newspapers criticised the chamber for closing the meeting to the public and accused members of seeking to insulate themselves from pro-democracy critics who had planned to pack the public seats.
A spokesman for the Provisional Legislature dismissed the suggestions and said it was merely a matter of space.
